children: Regulators say Amazon secretly inflated advertising prices and extracted more than $20 billion. The company says the lawsuit misunderstands how its auctions work.
FTC package arrives
Amazon shares
dropped 2.5% Monday after the Federal Trade Commission and 22 US states sued the company over its advertising practices.
Regulators are seeking tens of billions of dollars in damages, refunds and penalties. That qualifies as more than the usual cost of doing business.
The lawsuit alleges Amazon secretly increased the minimum prices advertisers paid to promote products, affecting more than 1.2 million customers since 2019.
Those advertisers included over 500,000 small and medium-sized businesses already competing for visibility inside Amazon’s increasingly pay-to-play marketplace.
Regulators claim the practices extracted more than $20 billion from advertisers and ultimately raised consumer prices as sellers passed along their higher marketing costs.
These remain allegations, and no court has determined that Amazon acted unlawfully. Amazon called the case misguided and promised to defend itself.
Ad auctions face scrutiny
Amazon typically describes its system as a second-price auction. Advertisers bid for placement, but the winner should pay only slightly more than the second-highest offer.
The FTC alleges Amazon inserted undisclosed prices into those auctions, effectively charging winners more than genuine competition required.
The complaint also says Amazon gradually increased surcharges before high-traffic events such as Prime Day and Black Friday to make the changes less noticeable.
Regulators cited internal discussions describing the mechanism as a non-transparent but effective method of increasing revenue. Subtle wording; rather less subtle legal exposure.

Amazon disputes that interpretation. The company says average winning search-ad bids fell by about 50% between 2019 and 2024 and argues its adjustments saved advertisers $8 billion from 2021 through 2025. Two very different calculations have now booked the same courtroom.
The quiet profit engine matters
Amazon generated $68.6 billion in advertising sales during 2025, making it the world’s third-largest digital ad platform behind Google and Meta.
Second-quarter ad revenue increased 26% to $19.8 billion — considerably faster than the company’s online-store business.

Advertising is generally more profitable than storing, packaging and delivering physical goods. Forced refunds would hurt immediately, while changes to auction pricing could reduce future revenue per ad. The larger investor risk is therefore structural, not merely another one-time settlement.
Amazon previously paid $2.5 billion to resolve FTC claims involving Prime subscriptions and still faces a separate marketplace antitrust case.

and whether advertisers pursue private claims. One regulator is manageable; 22 states and 1.2 million customers make a busier inbox.
